Updated assessment with SLOOS context:
- Policy stance remains highly accommodative (ELB, ongoing Treasury/MBS purchases, AIT framework), supporting growth and allowing inflation to run moderately above 2% for a time.
- SLOOS signals improving credit supply: banks eased standards for residential real estate (including HELOCs and GSE-eligible mortgages) and for consumer credit (credit cards, auto, general consumer), with reduced minimum credit score requirements. Large banks eased standards for investment‑grade firms. This supports the FOMC’s goal of maintaining accommodative financial conditions and improving the flow of credit to households and businesses.
- Still‑present frictions: relative to pre‑pandemic, some standards remain tighter; some large banks tightened certain C&I loan policies; foreign banks kept standards unchanged for IG firms but tightened for below‑IG firms. These nuances, alongside FSR‑highlighted vulnerabilities (elevated valuations, nonbank fragilities, short‑term funding sensitivities), temper the outlook.
- Net: Compared with the prior FSR‑only view, SLOOS points to a more supportive credit backdrop, especially for households and higher‑quality borrowers, modestly improving the growth outlook while leaving tail risks intact.
